items.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: The intensity of certain players, Muggsy Spanier and the beautiful intensity of Ruby Braff. Those are probably the strongest influences on me.

ctx.x: Were your tastes changing at all as you went along? Let’s say by the time you graduated you were in your early 20s. Your tastes pretty much stayed with the traditional jazz at that time?

Well it paid my way through school so I knew it had an economic thing. And Dixieland or New York Swing, Eddie Condon stuff had a resurgence in the ‘50s, and so I stayed with that because it was very popular at all the colleges. And since it was still popular for me, as soon as I graduated college I still gravitated to the Condon kind of guys. I sat in and played and subbed at Condon’s a couple of times. Most of my gigs were — I don’t like the word traditional but I guess it’s so long ago that people call it…

You must have occasion where you try to explain the differences — what there are — between New Orleans Dixieland, Chicago jazz and New York swing as you called it. Can you explain it to me? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
